screens.title: Arrays and Data Collection
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn how fixed-size arrays and simple structures let an embedded program collect, store, and organize sensor data reliably. Arrays are consecutive memory slots for values of the same type. That linear layout makes indexing and iteration fast and compact, but it also forces you to choose sizes carefully on devices with tight memory. You will see how to declare arrays of integers, how to group related fields into a structure, and how to pass arrays to functions so the data can be processed in place. We will also study circular buffers, a practical pattern that keeps only the most recent samples by advancing head and tail indexes and wrapping around the buffer. As a concrete example, you will follow a hands-on scenario that samples a switch every one hundred milliseconds into a ring buffer of sixty-four slots, then dumps the history to a serial console and measures average timing between presses. Along the way, common mistakes such as off-by-one indexing, buffer overruns, and incorrect pointer uses are highlighted with corrective patterns. By the end, you should be able to pick an array size, implement a simple ring buffer, and pass your collected data into processing functions for aggregation or transmission.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to declare and use arrays of integers and structures in C, and do so with the constraints of embedded memory in mind. You will set up arrays to store sequences like sensor readings and system states, and you'll implement circular buffers that continuously record the most recent samples by wrapping indexes. You will confidently pass arrays to functions by sending a pointer to the first element, letting the function modify the data in place or compute aggregates and write results back. Practically, you will complete a lab that samples a switch every one hundred milliseconds into a sixty-four-element ring buffer, dumps the buffer to a serial console, and computes an average. These objectives matter because embedded devices often cannot use dynamic memory or large allocations; fixed arrays and ring buffers offer predictable memory usage and simple real-time behavior. A final objective is understanding common pitfalls: off-by-one errors, buffer overruns, and misused pointers. With this skill set you can build robust data collection routines for small microcontrollers and reason about memory usage and timing behavior.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical Outcomes
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide emphasizes practical outcomes and safety checks. You will configure arrays to hold sensor readings and decide element type and size based on range and frequency. You will implement a ring buffer that advances a head index and updates the tail when overwriting oldest data, so your system never blocks when memory is full. You will design functions that accept a pointer and size so aggregation, filtering, or transmission can be implemented without copying large buffers. You will also learn to recognize off-by-one errors, boundary violations, and the dangers of using sizes that exceed available R A M. A concrete example: selecting sixty-four slots for a one-hundred-millisecond sample interval gives you 6.4 seconds of history; you should verify that fits your memory budget. Finally, you will practice a small lab: sample a switch at one hundred milliseconds into a sixty-four element circular buffer, dump via UART after ten seconds, and compute the average interval between press events. Knowing these outcomes ensures your designs are predictable, testable, and safe on constrained microcontrollers.

screens.title: What is an array in C?
screens.narratorSegment: An array is a fixed-size, contiguous block of memory that holds multiple values of the same type. In C, declaring an array reserves enough memory for the specified number of elements; the compiler does not automatically grow the array. For embedded systems this predictability is important because memory is limited and deterministic allocation avoids fragmentation. A typical declaration for unsigned 32-bit sensor values looks like: uint32_t sensorData[100]; That reserves space for one hundred elements and indexing starts at zero. You read or write an element with sensorData[0] or sensorData[99]. Iteration is usually done with a for loop that increments an index and directly accesses each slot. A common misconception is to assume array bounds are checked; in standard C there is no runtime check, so writing past the last index overwrites adjacent memory and can cause subtle faults. A small example: filling an array with readings at one-second intervals lets you keep a short history in R A M; choose element type and count based on value range and total memory available. Takeaway: arrays give simple, fast indexed access and predictable memory layout, but they require careful sizing and boundary discipline to avoid corrupting other data.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: An array is contiguous memory for same-typed elements; no automatic bounds checking in C.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › What is an array in C?
Array declaration and access
Fixed-size slot container in contiguous memory; index starts at zero.
// Reserve 100 unsigned 32-bit samples
uint32_t sensorData[100];

// Write samples
sensorData[0] = 42;
sensorData[1] = 55;

// Iterate
for (uint32_t i = 0; i < 100; i++) {
    sensorData[i] = readSensor();
}
Example
Storing one hundred temperature readings sampled once per second gives a predictable minute-and-forty history.
Common mistake
Assuming the language checks bounds. Writing past the last index corrupts memory and leads to unpredictable failures.
Key Takeaway

Arrays provide compact, predictable storage. Always ensure your index stays within declared size.

Memory layout visualization
Notice that the array's index labels map directly to consecutive memory. That mapping makes pointer arithmetic predictable: array plus offset leads to the correct element address, and lack of bounds checking is a safety cost we must manage.

screens.title: Indexing and Iteration
screens.narratorSegment: Iteration over array elements is the canonical way to fill or process sensor histories. The typical pattern uses a for loop with an unsigned integer index that runs from zero up to, but not including, the declared size. This loop structure guarantees you visit each element exactly once when the bounds are correct. For embedded code prefer explicit size constants or macros instead of magic numbers so the loop condition follows the declaration. For example, defining BUFFER_SIZE and using i less than BUFFER_SIZE keeps code consistent. A common example is filling an array with sensor readings inside a timed loop. One practical tip: prefer uint32_t or other unsigned counters when the size is non-negative; mixing signed and unsigned comparisons can be a source of bugs. A common misconception is to use less-than-or-equal instead of less-than when iterating to the last element — that off-by-one causes an out-of-bounds write. Another pattern is to compute a running aggregate while iterating rather than storing all values, if you only need an average; that saves memory. Concrete example: if you need both history and average, fill the array and compute the sum in the same loop, then divide. Check your loop invariants and prefer clear constants to reduce the chance of off-by-one errors.

keyIdea.title: Iteration Pattern
keyIdea.text: Use explicit size constants and less-than conditions to avoid off-by-one errors when iterating arrays.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Indexing and Iteration
For-loop pattern
Use a defined size and less-than comparison to visit every slot safely.
#define BUFFER_SIZE 100
uint32_t sensorData[BUFFER_SIZE];

for (uint32_t i = 0; i < BUFFER_SIZE; i++) {
    sensorData[i] = readSensor();
    sum += sensorData[i];
}

uint32_t average = sum / BUFFER_SIZE;
Pro tip
Compute aggregates during the same loop when possible to avoid reading the array twice and improve cache locality.
Misconception
Using i <= BUFFER_SIZE mistakenly writes one past the end. Always use less-than with the declared size.
Example scenario
Sampling a light sensor every 200 milliseconds into an array of fifty elements stores ten seconds of history. Using a BUFFER_SIZE macro makes future changes consistent across declaration, loop, and functions.
When to avoid storing
If you only need an average, compute sum on the fly and avoid the array entirely to save memory.
When to store
Store history when you must analyze sample patterns or replay recent events after an interrupt.
Key Takeaway

Use explicit size constants and less-than loop conditions to iterate safely and avoid off-by-one errors.

screens.title: Structures and arrays of structures
screens.narratorSegment: Structures provide a way to group related fields into a single compound type. In data collection, each sensor sample may include a timestamp, the measured value, and a small status flag. Defining a typedef struct for SensorReading makes code clearer and avoids parallel arrays. For example, a SensorReading with a 32-bit timestamp, 32-bit value, and an 8-bit status fits into compact memory, and an array of fifty such structures reserves fifty contiguous records. Using arrays of structures improves locality: each record's fields live next to each other in memory, which is convenient when processing a sample at a time. A typical declaration looks like typedef struct { uint32_t timestamp; uint32_t value; uint8_t status; } SensorReading; SensorReading readings[50]; A common misconception is assuming structures add significant runtime overhead. They are simply a layout in memory; the compiler arranges fields and padding, so being mindful of alignment reduces wasted bytes. Practical tip: order fields to minimize padding, and prefer fixed-width integer types to make storage predictable across platforms. Takeaway question: how would you change the structure if you needed a 16-bit value instead of 32-bit to save memory?

keyIdea.text: Use typedef structs to represent a sample with timestamp, value, and status; arrays of structs improve locality and clarity.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Structures and arrays of structures
Structure declaration
A structure groups related fields so each sample is a single record.
typedef struct {
    uint32_t timestamp;
    uint32_t value;
    uint8_t  status;
} SensorReading;

SensorReading readings[50];
Example
Each array element is a complete sample: timestamp plus value plus status makes processing simpler and clearer than parallel arrays.
Pro tip
Order fields from largest to smallest to reduce padding or explicitly use packed attributes only when alignment is acceptable for your CPU.
Array of structures visualization
Record 0
timestamp | value | status
Record 1
timestamp | value | status
Processing one record at a time avoids scattered memory accesses and keeps code readable: readings[i].value is clear and compact. Consider size and alignment when designing the struct for minimal RAM usage.
Key Takeaway

Structures make grouped samples explicit and arrays of structs give contiguous records for easier per-sample processing.

screens.title: Passing arrays to functions
screens.narratorSegment: In C, arrays decay to pointers when passed to functions, so you pass the address of the first element and a size parameter to let the function know how many elements to process. This approach avoids copying large memory blocks and allows the called function to modify the caller's data directly. For example, a function that calculates an average can accept a uint32_t pointer, the size, and a pointer to the result so it writes the aggregate back to the caller. When you write such functions, always document whether the pointer may be NULL and whether the function writes to the passed buffer. A common pitfall is forgetting to pass the correct size; if the size is larger than the actual array, the function may read memory beyond the allocation. Another subtlety is const-correctness: mark the pointer as const when the function should not modify the data. Concrete example: a calculateAverage function takes data, size, and result pointer, sums elements in a loop, and then stores the average to *result. Takeaway: always pass the element count explicitly and prefer clear pointer signatures to prevent misuse and undefined behavior.

keyIdea.title: Function Interface
keyIdea.text: Pass a pointer to element zero and an explicit size; document mutability and nullability for safe in-place operations.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Passing arrays to functions
Signature pattern
Pass pointer to first element, size, and a pointer for output if needed.
void calculateAverage(uint32_t *data, uint32_t size, uint32_t *result) {
    uint32_t sum = 0;
    for (uint32_t i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        sum += data[i];
    }
    *result = sum / size;
}

// Caller:
uint32_t values[10];
uint32_t avg;
calculateAverage(values, 10, &avg);
Example
This pattern computes an average without copying the array; the function writes the result back through the result pointer.
Pitfall
If size is zero or larger than the real array, the function will divide by zero or read out-of-bounds. Always validate inputs at the call and in the function.
Const correctness and documentation
When the function must not modify the buffer, declare the pointer const. Document whether null pointers are allowed and whether size zero is valid to make safe calling contracts.
Check Your Understanding

What happens if you pass an array and an incorrect size? Hint: reading beyond allocation leads to undefined behavior.

screens.title: calculateAverage example explained
screens.narratorSegment: Let's examine the calculateAverage pattern step-by-step and highlight defensive checks you should add. The function receives a pointer to data, a size, and a pointer for the result. It initializes a sum variable, iterates from zero to size minus one, accumulates elements, and computes the integer average by dividing sum by size. Important runtime concerns: check that the pointers are not NULL and that size is non-zero before dividing. In embedded C use unsigned types for counters and be mindful of potential overflow of the running sum when many large samples are added. If overflow is possible, choose a wider accumulator or perform scaled averaging. For example, when summing one hundred 32-bit readings the sum could exceed 32 bits, so you might use a 64-bit accumulator if available. A misconception is expecting floating-point averages without explicit conversion; integer division discards fractions. If you need precision, convert to a fixed-point representation or compute with a float only when hardware supports efficient floating arithmetic. Takeaway: add input checks, consider accumulator width, and document whether the function modifies data or may block. Example question: how would you protect the function against size equal to zero?

keyIdea.title: Defensive Coding
keyIdea.text: Validate pointers and size, consider accumulator width to avoid overflow, and be explicit about integer division behavior.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › calculateAverage example explained
Secure version
void calculateAverage(const uint32_t *data, uint32_t size, uint32_t *result) {
    if (data == NULL || result == NULL || size == 0) return; // defensive
    uint64_t sum = 0; // wider accumulator to avoid overflow
    for (uint32_t i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        sum += data[i];
    }
    *result = (uint32_t)(sum / size); // integer average
}
Note the defensive null checks and the use of a 64-bit accumulator to reduce overflow risk on many 32-bit additions.
Practical considerations
  • Validate size is non-zero to avoid division by zero.
  • Use wider accumulator if element values can sum beyond the accumulator width.
  • Remember integer division truncates; use fixed-point or float if you need fractions.
Check
Would a 64-bit accumulator be available on your MCU? If not, design scaled averaging or periodic subtraction to avoid overflow.

screens.title: Circular buffer (ring buffer) concept
screens.narratorSegment: A circular buffer, also called a ring buffer, is a fixed-size array used as a circular queue where new writes advance a head index and reads advance a tail index. When the head reaches the end of the backing array it wraps to zero using modulo arithmetic. If the head catches the tail on a write, the oldest data is overwritten and the tail is advanced as well. This pattern is excellent for continuous data collection where only a sliding window of recent samples is needed and memory must remain bounded. A common embedded use is storing recent sensor readings for diagnostics or for smoothing filters. Concrete example: a buffer with BUFFER_SIZE sixty-four holds the last sixty-four switch samples; each write sets buffer[head] and then head equals head plus one modulo BUFFER_SIZE. A common misconception is assuming the ring will block writers when full; a basic circular buffer usually overwrites oldest data instead of blocking. If blocking behavior is required, a different queue or synchronization mechanism must be used. Takeaway: rings give predictable bounded memory for streaming data, but you must decide whether overwriting or blocking semantics suit your application.

keyIdea.title: Ring Concept
keyIdea.text: A fixed-size array with head and tail indexes that wrap; it overwrites oldest data when full unless explicitly designed to block.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Circular buffer (ring buffer) concept
Ring buffer essentials
Head advances on write, tail advances on read, both wrap using modulo arithmetic.
State
Keep two indexes: head for next write and tail for next read. When head equals tail the buffer is empty; on write if head reaches tail, advance tail to overwrite oldest data.
Wrap
Use head = (head + 1) % BUFFER_SIZE to wrap. This guarantees head stays within bounds and simplifies logic.
Example
A 64-slot ring sampled every 100 milliseconds keeps 6.4 seconds of recent data without dynamic allocation.
Misconception
Rings do not automatically prevent data loss; deciding to overwrite oldest data is a deliberate design choice.

screens.title: Circular buffer implementation
screens.narratorSegment: Here is the classic circular buffer implementation pattern with a fixed-size backing array, a head index, and a tail index. On write, the value is stored at buffer[head], head is incremented and wrapped using modulo BUFFER_SIZE, and if head equals tail we advance tail as well to indicate the oldest data was overwritten. On read, if tail equals head the buffer is empty; otherwise read buffer[tail] and advance tail with modulo. This implementation offers constant-time writes and reads with predictable memory usage. Example code defines BUFFER_SIZE, declares buffer, head, and tail, and then provides bufferWrite and bufferRead functions. A common mistake is failing to use modulo consistently or using signed arithmetic in a way that makes wrap logic incorrect when subtracting indexes. Another subtle bug arises when multiple tasks or interrupts access the ring; you must protect concurrent access with atomic operations, disabling interrupts briefly, or using a lock if OS primitives are available. For simple single-producer single-consumer scenarios on microcontrollers, careful ordering and volatile qualifiers often suffice. Takeaway: keep wrap logic simple, validate concurrency requirements, and document whether writes overwrite or block.

keyIdea.title: Implementation
keyIdea.text: Write stores at head, increments with modulo, and advances tail on overwrite; read advances tail and must detect empty state.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Circular buffer implementation
Ring buffer code
#define BUFFER_SIZE 64

uint32_t buffer[BUFFER_SIZE];
uint32_t head = 0;
uint32_t tail = 0;

void bufferWrite(uint32_t value) {
    buffer[head] = value;
    head = (head + 1) % BUFFER_SIZE;
    if (head == tail) {
        tail = (tail + 1) % BUFFER_SIZE; // overwrite oldest
    }
}

uint32_t bufferRead(void) {
    if (tail == head) {
        return 0; // buffer empty
    }
    uint32_t value = buffer[tail];
    tail = (tail + 1) % BUFFER_SIZE;
    return value;
}
This implementation uses modulo to wrap indexes and advances tail to preserve the most recent BUFFER_SIZE items when writes overtake reads.
Concurrency considerations
  • Single producer and single consumer may be safe with volatile indexing and careful ordering.
  • Multiple writers or readers require atomic operations or disabling interrupts briefly during index updates.
  • Document whether reads return a special empty code or block until data arrives.
Key Takeaway

Use modulo for wrap, advance tail on overwrite, and protect concurrent access according to your system's needs.

screens.title: Overwrite vs blocking semantics
screens.narratorSegment: When designing a circular buffer you must decide whether writes will overwrite the oldest data when full or whether writers should block or be rejected. Overwrite semantics are simple and ensure continuous logging without backpressure; they are a good fit for diagnostics or non-critical telemetry where only recent samples matter. Blocking or rejecting writes preserves all data but introduces complexity: writers may need to wait, drop data upstream, or require synchronization. Consider an embedded switch logger: losing old history is acceptable if you care only about recent presses, so overwrite is fine. Conversely, a data acquisition system that must not lose samples should use a larger buffer, flow control, or an error-reporting mechanism so the producer knows a sample was dropped. A misconception is thinking overwrite always means silent loss; your code can set a flag when an overwrite occurs so downstream logic knows the buffer rolled over. Practical rule: pick overwrite for bounded, continuous sampling and pick blocking or reporting for critical logging where each sample must be preserved. Closing question: what does your system do if a sensor spikes faster than your processing can handle?

Design trade-offs
Decide whether continuous logging or guaranteed capture matters more for your system.
Overwrite
  • No blocking, predictable memory usage.
  • Best for telemetry, diagnostics, and sliding windows.
  • Optionally set an overwrite flag so code knows data was lost.
Blocking / Reject
  • Preserves all samples at the cost of complexity.
  • Requires flow control, signaling, or increased buffer sizes.
  • Better for critical acquisition or packet capture.
Check

Which policy fits your application? If you can tolerate missing older samples, choose overwrite. If you cannot, design flow control or enlarge buffers.

screens.title: Lab: sample a switch into a ring buffer
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on scenario ties together declarations, ring behavior, and function passing. The lab samples a switch state every one hundred milliseconds and writes the Boolean value into a sixty-four element circular buffer. After ten seconds the system dumps the buffer contents to the serial console and then calculates the average time between detected press events. Start by defining BUFFER_SIZE equal to sixty-four and the buffer variable as uint32_t or a smaller type if only storing booleans. Implement bufferWrite according to the ring pattern, and a dump function that reads until the buffer is empty and prints each entry. To compute average time between presses, scan the dumped values and record timestamps when transitions from not-pressed to pressed occur, compute differences, and average them. A frequent mistake is sampling too quickly relative to debounce time, which results in many false press entries; include debouncing logic or sample at a rate appropriate for the switch. Another potential issue is using a buffering type that wastes memory; choose the smallest sufficient integer type. Takeaway: practice gives confidence—implement the ring, verify wrap-around behavior, and ensure UART output shows the expected sliding window of recent samples.

screens.title: Finding maximum and understanding pointer equivalence
screens.narratorSegment: A simple assessment reinforces indexing and pointer equivalence. Given a ten-element array initialized to {5, 3, 8, 1, 9, 2, 7, 4, 6, 0}, write a function that finds the maximum value and its index. This exercise teaches iteration, comparison, and returning or communicating results via pointers or structures. The function may iterate with an index i, track current max and its index, and update them when a larger value is found. A second question asks what is the difference between array[i] and *(array + i). In standard C they are equivalent: both access the element at offset i from the start pointer. A common misconception is thinking pointer notation is a different operation; it is the same memory access expressed differently. For embedded work, prefer the clearer array[i] form when possible for readability. When returning both value and index, either return a struct with both fields or write to pointers provided by the caller. This assessment consolidates array traversal, comparison, and pointer semantics in a single practical task. Finding maximum and understanding pointer equivalence means practice max-finding logic and remember array[i] and *(array + i) are the same access in c.. In practical terms, array indexing versus pointer arithmetic and a small assessment task. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Sizing arrays and avoiding overflow
screens.narratorSegment: Selecting array sizes and types is fundamental to reliable embedded design. First, choose the smallest type that can hold your data to save R A M; for binary switch state a uint8_t is adequate, while timestamps may need 32-bit values. Structures should be ordered to reduce padding: place larger fields first. Always use named constants for sizes and check indexes before writing. Avoid dynamic allocation on many small MCUs; fixed-size arrays give predictable stack and static memory footprints. Another important point is to document the memory cost in bytes for each buffer so you can verify the total fits available R A M. When summing multiple elements, choose an accumulator that can hold the maximum possible sum. For concurrency, mark shared indices volatile and protect index updates if interrupts or multiple tasks access the buffer. A frequent mistake is forgetting to consider alignment and padding in structures, which can waste bytes. Closing question: can you reduce an array's memory by switching from uint32_t to uint16_t without losing necessary range? Test your choice against realistic data ranges before changing types. Sizing arrays and avoiding overflow means pick compact types, use named size constants, validate indexes, and plan accumulators to prevent overflow.. In practical terms, choose types, minimize padding, and validate indices. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Sizing checklist
Choose types
Prefer the smallest integer width that preserves range. For timestamps, use 32-bit when needed; for flags, use 8-bit.
Document cost
Calculate bytes used and verify against available static RAM; update documentation if sizes change.
Accumulator
Use a wider accumulator for sums to prevent overflow when aggregating many elements.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's recap the most important ideas. First, arrays are contiguous fixed-size containers with index starting at zero. They are efficient and predictable but have no runtime bounds checks, so validate indexes. Second, structures group related fields like timestamp, value, and status, and arrays of structures keep records contiguous for per-sample processing. Third, circular buffers provide a simple way to retain the most recent N samples by advancing head and tail with modulo arithmetic; choose overwrite or blocking behavior based on application needs. Additionally, when passing arrays to functions, pass a pointer to element zero plus an explicit size and validate inputs. Finally, be intentional with type widths and accumulator sizes to prevent overflow and to fit within limited embedded R A M. These concepts form the basis for robust sensor logging and small-memory analytics on microcontrollers. Keep these rules in mind when designing collection routines and choose patterns that match your device's timing and memory constraints.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn how fixed-size arrays and simple structures let an embedded program collect, store, and organize sensor data reliably. Arrays are consecutive memory slots for values of the same type. That linear layout makes indexing and iteration fast and compact, but it also forces you to choose sizes carefully on devices with tight memory. You will see how to declare arrays of integers, how to group related fields into a structure, and how to pass arrays to functions so the data can be processed in place. We will also study circular buffers, a practical pattern that keeps only the most recent samples by advancing head and tail indexes and wrapping around the buffer. As a concrete example, you will follow a hands-on scenario that samples a switch every one hundred milliseconds into a ring buffer of sixty-four slots, then dumps the history to a serial console and measures average timing between presses. Along the way, common mistakes such as off-by-one indexing, buffer overruns, and incorrect pointer uses are highlighted with corrective patterns. By the end, you should be able to pick an array size, implement a simple ring buffer, and pass your collected data into processing functions for aggregation or transmission.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to declare and use arrays of integers and structures in C, and do so with the constraints of embedded memory in mind. You will set up arrays to store sequences like sensor readings and system states, and you'll implement circular buffers that continuously record the most recent samples by wrapping indexes. You will confidently pass arrays to functions by sending a pointer to the first element, letting the function modify the data in place or compute aggregates and write results back. Practically, you will complete a lab that samples a switch every one hundred milliseconds into a sixty-four-element ring buffer, dumps the buffer to a serial console, and computes an average. These objectives matter because embedded devices often cannot use dynamic memory or large allocations; fixed arrays and ring buffers offer predictable memory usage and simple real-time behavior. A final objective is understanding common pitfalls: off-by-one errors, buffer overruns, and misused pointers. With this skill set you can build robust data collection routines for small microcontrollers and reason about memory usage and timing behavior.

This second objectives slide emphasizes practical outcomes and safety checks. You will configure arrays to hold sensor readings and decide element type and size based on range and frequency. You will implement a ring buffer that advances a head index and updates the tail when overwriting oldest data, so your system never blocks when memory is full. You will design functions that accept a pointer and size so aggregation, filtering, or transmission can be implemented without copying large buffers. You will also learn to recognize off-by-one errors, boundary violations, and the dangers of using sizes that exceed available R A M. A concrete example: selecting sixty-four slots for a one-hundred-millisecond sample interval gives you 6.4 seconds of history; you should verify that fits your memory budget. Finally, you will practice a small lab: sample a switch at one hundred milliseconds into a sixty-four element circular buffer, dump via UART after ten seconds, and compute the average interval between press events. Knowing these outcomes ensures your designs are predictable, testable, and safe on constrained microcontrollers.

An array is a fixed-size, contiguous block of memory that holds multiple values of the same type. In C, declaring an array reserves enough memory for the specified number of elements; the compiler does not automatically grow the array. For embedded systems this predictability is important because memory is limited and deterministic allocation avoids fragmentation. A typical declaration for unsigned 32-bit sensor values looks like: uint32_t sensorData[100]; That reserves space for one hundred elements and indexing starts at zero. You read or write an element with sensorData[0] or sensorData[99]. Iteration is usually done with a for loop that increments an index and directly accesses each slot. A common misconception is to assume array bounds are checked; in standard C there is no runtime check, so writing past the last index overwrites adjacent memory and can cause subtle faults. A small example: filling an array with readings at one-second intervals lets you keep a short history in R A M; choose element type and count based on value range and total memory available. Takeaway: arrays give simple, fast indexed access and predictable memory layout, but they require careful sizing and boundary discipline to avoid corrupting other data.

Iteration over array elements is the canonical way to fill or process sensor histories. The typical pattern uses a for loop with an unsigned integer index that runs from zero up to, but not including, the declared size. This loop structure guarantees you visit each element exactly once when the bounds are correct. For embedded code prefer explicit size constants or macros instead of magic numbers so the loop condition follows the declaration. For example, defining BUFFER_SIZE and using i less than BUFFER_SIZE keeps code consistent. A common example is filling an array with sensor readings inside a timed loop. One practical tip: prefer uint32_t or other unsigned counters when the size is non-negative; mixing signed and unsigned comparisons can be a source of bugs. A common misconception is to use less-than-or-equal instead of less-than when iterating to the last element — that off-by-one causes an out-of-bounds write. Another pattern is to compute a running aggregate while iterating rather than storing all values, if you only need an average; that saves memory. Concrete example: if you need both history and average, fill the array and compute the sum in the same loop, then divide. Check your loop invariants and prefer clear constants to reduce the chance of off-by-one errors.

Structures provide a way to group related fields into a single compound type. In data collection, each sensor sample may include a timestamp, the measured value, and a small status flag. Defining a typedef struct for SensorReading makes code clearer and avoids parallel arrays. For example, a SensorReading with a 32-bit timestamp, 32-bit value, and an 8-bit status fits into compact memory, and an array of fifty such structures reserves fifty contiguous records. Using arrays of structures improves locality: each record's fields live next to each other in memory, which is convenient when processing a sample at a time. A typical declaration looks like typedef struct { uint32_t timestamp; uint32_t value; uint8_t status; } SensorReading; SensorReading readings[50]; A common misconception is assuming structures add significant runtime overhead. They are simply a layout in memory; the compiler arranges fields and padding, so being mindful of alignment reduces wasted bytes. Practical tip: order fields to minimize padding, and prefer fixed-width integer types to make storage predictable across platforms. Takeaway question: how would you change the structure if you needed a 16-bit value instead of 32-bit to save memory?

In C, arrays decay to pointers when passed to functions, so you pass the address of the first element and a size parameter to let the function know how many elements to process. This approach avoids copying large memory blocks and allows the called function to modify the caller's data directly. For example, a function that calculates an average can accept a uint32_t pointer, the size, and a pointer to the result so it writes the aggregate back to the caller. When you write such functions, always document whether the pointer may be NULL and whether the function writes to the passed buffer. A common pitfall is forgetting to pass the correct size; if the size is larger than the actual array, the function may read memory beyond the allocation. Another subtlety is const-correctness: mark the pointer as const when the function should not modify the data. Concrete example: a calculateAverage function takes data, size, and result pointer, sums elements in a loop, and then stores the average to *result. Takeaway: always pass the element count explicitly and prefer clear pointer signatures to prevent misuse and undefined behavior.

Let's examine the calculateAverage pattern step-by-step and highlight defensive checks you should add. The function receives a pointer to data, a size, and a pointer for the result. It initializes a sum variable, iterates from zero to size minus one, accumulates elements, and computes the integer average by dividing sum by size. Important runtime concerns: check that the pointers are not NULL and that size is non-zero before dividing. In embedded C use unsigned types for counters and be mindful of potential overflow of the running sum when many large samples are added. If overflow is possible, choose a wider accumulator or perform scaled averaging. For example, when summing one hundred 32-bit readings the sum could exceed 32 bits, so you might use a 64-bit accumulator if available. A misconception is expecting floating-point averages without explicit conversion; integer division discards fractions. If you need precision, convert to a fixed-point representation or compute with a float only when hardware supports efficient floating arithmetic. Takeaway: add input checks, consider accumulator width, and document whether the function modifies data or may block. Example question: how would you protect the function against size equal to zero?

A circular buffer, also called a ring buffer, is a fixed-size array used as a circular queue where new writes advance a head index and reads advance a tail index. When the head reaches the end of the backing array it wraps to zero using modulo arithmetic. If the head catches the tail on a write, the oldest data is overwritten and the tail is advanced as well. This pattern is excellent for continuous data collection where only a sliding window of recent samples is needed and memory must remain bounded. A common embedded use is storing recent sensor readings for diagnostics or for smoothing filters. Concrete example: a buffer with BUFFER_SIZE sixty-four holds the last sixty-four switch samples; each write sets buffer[head] and then head equals head plus one modulo BUFFER_SIZE. A common misconception is assuming the ring will block writers when full; a basic circular buffer usually overwrites oldest data instead of blocking. If blocking behavior is required, a different queue or synchronization mechanism must be used. Takeaway: rings give predictable bounded memory for streaming data, but you must decide whether overwriting or blocking semantics suit your application.

Here is the classic circular buffer implementation pattern with a fixed-size backing array, a head index, and a tail index. On write, the value is stored at buffer[head], head is incremented and wrapped using modulo BUFFER_SIZE, and if head equals tail we advance tail as well to indicate the oldest data was overwritten. On read, if tail equals head the buffer is empty; otherwise read buffer[tail] and advance tail with modulo. This implementation offers constant-time writes and reads with predictable memory usage. Example code defines BUFFER_SIZE, declares buffer, head, and tail, and then provides bufferWrite and bufferRead functions. A common mistake is failing to use modulo consistently or using signed arithmetic in a way that makes wrap logic incorrect when subtracting indexes. Another subtle bug arises when multiple tasks or interrupts access the ring; you must protect concurrent access with atomic operations, disabling interrupts briefly, or using a lock if OS primitives are available. For simple single-producer single-consumer scenarios on microcontrollers, careful ordering and volatile qualifiers often suffice. Takeaway: keep wrap logic simple, validate concurrency requirements, and document whether writes overwrite or block.

When designing a circular buffer you must decide whether writes will overwrite the oldest data when full or whether writers should block or be rejected. Overwrite semantics are simple and ensure continuous logging without backpressure; they are a good fit for diagnostics or non-critical telemetry where only recent samples matter. Blocking or rejecting writes preserves all data but introduces complexity: writers may need to wait, drop data upstream, or require synchronization. Consider an embedded switch logger: losing old history is acceptable if you care only about recent presses, so overwrite is fine. Conversely, a data acquisition system that must not lose samples should use a larger buffer, flow control, or an error-reporting mechanism so the producer knows a sample was dropped. A misconception is thinking overwrite always means silent loss; your code can set a flag when an overwrite occurs so downstream logic knows the buffer rolled over. Practical rule: pick overwrite for bounded, continuous sampling and pick blocking or reporting for critical logging where each sample must be preserved. Closing question: what does your system do if a sensor spikes faster than your processing can handle?
